claim: The malaria parasite Plasmodium falciparum synthesizes significant amounts of phospholipids to meet the demands of replication within red blood cells.
source: The malaria parasite Plasmodium falciparum synthesizes significant amounts of phospholipids to meet the demands of replication within red blood cells.
evidence: This is a general statement about parasite biology that is supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: De novo phosphatidylcholine (PC) biosynthesis via the Kennedy pathway is essential for P. falciparum.
source: De novo phosphatidylcholine (PC) biosynthesis via the Kennedy pathway is essential, requiring choline that is primarily sourced from host serum lysophosphatidylcholine (lysoPC).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations and established knowledge about PC biosynthesis in the parasite.

claim: Choline required for PC synthesis is primarily sourced from host serum lysophosphatidylcholine (lysoPC).
source: De novo phosphatidylcholine (PC) biosynthesis via the Kennedy pathway is essential, requiring choline that is primarily sourced from host serum lysophosphatidylcholine (lysoPC).
evidence: This is supported by prior research cited in the manuscript.

claim: LysoPC acts as an environmental sensor to regulate parasite sexual differentiation.
source: LysoPC also acts as an environmental sensor to regulate parasite sexual differentiation.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The enzyme(s) involved in lysoPC breakdown to free choline for PC synthesis are unknown.
source: Despite these critical roles for host lysoPC, the enzyme(s) involved in its breakdown to free choline for PC synthesis are unknown.
evidence: This statement establishes the knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: A parasite glycerophosphodiesterase (PfGDPD) is indispensable for blood stage parasite proliferation.
source: Here, we show that a parasite glycerophosphodiesterase (PfGDPD) is indispensable for blood stage parasite proliferation.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Exogenous choline rescues growth of PfGDPD-null parasites.
source: Exogenous choline rescues growth of PfGDPD-null parasites, directly linking PfGDPD function to choline incorporation.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Genetic ablation of PfGDPD reduces choline uptake from lysoPC.
source: Genetic ablation of PfGDPD reduces choline uptake from lysoPC, resulting in depletion of several PC species in the parasite, whilst purified PfGDPD releases choline from glycerophosphocholine in vitro.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by metabolic labeling experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: Genetic ablation of PfGDPD results in depletion of several PC species in the parasite.
source: Genetic ablation of PfGDPD reduces choline uptake from lysoPC, resulting in depletion of several PC species in the parasite, whilst purified PfGDPD releases choline from glycerophosphocholine in vitro.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by lipidomic analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Purified PfGDPD releases choline from glycerophosphocholine in vitro.
source: Genetic ablation of PfGDPD reduces choline uptake from lysoPC, resulting in depletion of several PC species in the parasite, whilst purified PfGDPD releases choline from glycerophosphocholine in vitro.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by enzymatic assay data shown in Figure 6.

claim: PfGDPD is a choline-releasing glycerophosphodiesterase that mediates a critical step in PC biosynthesis and parasite survival.
source: Our results identify PfGDPD as a choline-releasing glycerophosphodiesterase that mediates a critical step in PC biosynthesis and parasite survival.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: During intraerythrocytic growth, the malaria parasite produces de novo large amounts of membrane to support expansion of its parasite plasma membrane (PPM), the parasitophorous vacuole membrane (PVM) and other membranous structures.
source: During its massive intraerythrocytic growth, the parasite produces de novo large amounts of membrane to support expansion of its parasite plasma membrane (PPM), the parasitophorous vacuole membrane (PVM) and other membranous structures of the growing parasite, as well as for formation of daughter merozoites.
evidence: This is established knowledge about parasite biology.

claim: Extensive membrane neogenesis culminates in a sixfold increase in the phospholipid content of the infected RBC.
source: This extensive membrane neogenesis, which culminates in a sixfold increase in the phospholipid content of the infected RBC (Wein et al., 2018), requires an intense phase of phospholipid synthesis during the metabolically active trophozoite and schizont stages of the parasite life cycle.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wein et al., 2018.

claim: Phosphatidylcholine (PC) is the most abundant membrane lipid in the malaria parasite, comprising 30–40% of total phospholipid.
source: Phosphatidylcholine (PC) is the most abundant membrane lipid in the malaria parasite, comprising 30–40% of total phospholipid (Botté et al., 2013; Gulati et al., 2015), and the parasite has evolved to produce this vital phospholipid via multiple enzymatic pathways from a variety of metabolic precursors from the host milieu (Wein et al., 2018; Kilian et al., 2018; Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Botté et al., 2013 and Gulati et al., 2015.

claim: Under normal conditions, ∼89% of PC is synthesized from free choline and fatty acids via the CDP-choline-dependent Kennedy pathway.
source: Under normal conditions, ∼89% of PC is synthesized from free choline and fatty acids via the CDP-choline-dependent Kennedy pathway that is common among eukaryotes (Brancucci et al., 2017; Wein et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Brancucci et al., 2017 and Wein et al., 2018.

claim: Choline is phosphorylated to phosphocholine (P-Cho) by choline kinase (CK).
source: Choline is phosphorylated to phosphocholine (P-Cho) by choline kinase (CK) (Ancelin and Vial, 1986b), then converted to CDP-choline by a CTP:phosphocholine cytidyltransferase (CCT) (Ancelin and Vial, 1989) and finally condensed with diacylglycerol (DAG) by a choline/ethanolamine-phosphotransferase (CEPT) (Vial et al., 1984) to produce PC.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ancelin and Vial, 1986b.

claim: P-Cho is converted to CDP-choline by a CTP:phosphocholine cytidyltransferase (CCT).
source: Choline is phosphorylated to phosphocholine (P-Cho) by choline kinase (CK) (Ancelin and Vial, 1986b), then converted to CDP-choline by a CTP:phosphocholine cytidyltransferase (CCT) (Ancelin and Vial, 1989) and finally condensed with diacylglycerol (DAG) by a choline/ethanolamine-phosphotransferase (CEPT) (Vial et al., 1984) to produce PC.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ancelin and Vial, 1989.

claim: CDP-choline is condensed with diacylglycerol (DAG) by a choline/ethanolamine-phosphotransferase (CEPT) to produce PC.
source: Choline is phosphorylated to phosphocholine (P-Cho) by choline kinase (CK) (Ancelin and Vial, 1986b), then converted to CDP-choline by a CTP:phosphocholine cytidyltransferase (CCT) (Ancelin and Vial, 1989) and finally condensed with diacylglycerol (DAG) by a choline/ethanolamine-phosphotransferase (CEPT) (Vial et al., 1984) to produce PC.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Vial et al., 1984.

claim: PC is also generated via an alternate serine-decarboxylase-phosphoethanolamine-methyltransferase (SDPM) pathway also found in plants and nematodes.
source: PC is also generated via an alternate serine-decarboxylase-phosphoethanolamine-methyltransferase (SDPM) pathway also found in plants and nematodes, that uses host serine and ethanolamine (Eth) as precursors (Pessi et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Pessi et al., 2004.

claim: In the SDPM pathway, precursor P-Cho is produced by triple methylation of phosphoethanolamine (P-Eth) by a phosphoethanolamine methyltransferase (PMT).
source: In this case, precursor P-Cho for the CDP-choline pathway is produced by triple methylation of phosphoethanolamine (P-Eth) by a phosphoethanolamine methyltransferase (PMT) (Witola et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Witola et al., 2008.

claim: Unlike yeast and mammals, the malaria parasite is unable to convert PE directly to PC through phospholipid methyl transferase activity.
source: Unlike yeast and mammals, the malaria parasite is unable to convert PE directly to PC through phospholipid methyl transferase activity (Witola et al., 2008), so the Kennedy and SDPM pathways intersect only at the point of PMT activity (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Witola et al., 2008.

claim: The Kennedy and SDPM pathways intersect only at the point of PMT activity.
source: Unlike yeast and mammals, the malaria parasite is unable to convert PE directly to PC through phospholipid methyl transferase activity (Witola et al., 2008), so the Kennedy and SDPM pathways intersect only at the point of PMT activity (Figure 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited literature and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: PC can be potentially produced by direct acylation of lysoPC via the Lands' cycle by an unknown lysophosphatidylcholine acyltransferase (LPCAT).
source: PC can also be potentially produced by direct acylation of lysoPC via the Lands' cycle by an unknown lysophosphatidylcholine acyltransferase (LPCAT).
evidence: This is based on knowledge of lipid metabolism pathways.

claim: The Lands' cycle pathway is considered to not contribute significantly to PC synthesis under normal conditions.
source: However, this pathway is considered to not contribute significantly to PC synthesis under normal conditions (Wein et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wein et al., 2018.

claim: Choline analogs have potent antimalarial activity.
source: Choline analogs have potent antimalarial activity (Ancelin et al., 2003), whilst inhibiting or disrupting enzymes in the PC synthesis pathways severely reduces or blocks intraerythrocytic growth.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ancelin et al., 2003.

claim: Inhibiting or disrupting enzymes in the PC synthesis pathways severely reduces or blocks intraerythrocytic growth.
source: Choline analogs have potent antimalarial activity (Ancelin et al., 2003), whilst inhibiting or disrupting enzymes in the PC synthesis pathways severely reduces or blocks intraerythrocytic growth.
evidence: This is supported by general knowledge and citations in the following sentences.

claim: Compounds that inhibit P. falciparum CK (PfCK) kill the parasite.
source: As examples of this, compounds that inhibit P. falciparum CK (PfCK) (Serrán-Aguilera et al., 2016) or PfCCT (Contet et al., 2015) in the CDP-choline pathway kill the parasite, and disruption of the PfPMT gene to block PC synthesis via the SDPM pathway results in morphological and growth defects but is not lethal (Witola et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Serrán-Aguilera et al., 2016.

claim: Compounds that inhibit PfCCT kill the parasite.
source: As examples of this, compounds that inhibit P. falciparum CK (PfCK) (Serrán-Aguilera et al., 2016) or PfCCT (Contet et al., 2015) in the CDP-choline pathway kill the parasite, and disruption of the PfPMT gene to block PC synthesis via the SDPM pathway results in morphological and growth defects but is not lethal (Witola et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Contet et al., 2015.

claim: Disruption of the PfPMT gene to block PC synthesis via the SDPM pathway results in morphological and growth defects but is not lethal.
source: As examples of this, compounds that inhibit P. falciparum CK (PfCK) (Serrán-Aguilera et al., 2016) or PfCCT (Contet et al., 2015) in the CDP-choline pathway kill the parasite, and disruption of the PfPMT gene to block PC synthesis via the SDPM pathway results in morphological and growth defects but is not lethal (Witola et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Witola et al., 2008.

claim: The CDP-choline pathway provides the major route to PC synthesis whilst the SDPM pathway forms an important alternative route.
source: These findings suggest that the CDP-choline pathway provides the major route to PC synthesis whilst the SDPM pathway forms an important alternative route.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited findings about enzyme inhibition and gene disruption.

claim: The choline required for PC synthesis is primarily scavenged from host serum.
source: The choline required for PC synthesis is primarily scavenged from host serum.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge and citations in the following sentences.

claim: Free choline can cross the PPM efficiently through an unidentified carrier.
source: Whilst free choline can cross the PPM efficiently through an unidentified carrier, choline transfer from serum into the infected RBC across the erythrocyte membrane via a parasite-induced new permeability pathway (NPP) appears rate-limiting (Ancelin and Vial, 1989; Biagini et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge.

claim: Choline transfer from serum into the infected RBC across the erythrocyte membrane via a parasite-induced new permeability pathway (NPP) appears rate-limiting.
source: Whilst free choline can cross the PPM efficiently through an unidentified carrier, choline transfer from serum into the infected RBC across the erythrocyte membrane via a parasite-induced new permeability pathway (NPP) appears rate-limiting (Ancelin and Vial, 1989; Biagini et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ancelin and Vial, 1989 and Biagini et al., 2004.

claim: The parasite has evolved to scavenge most of the required choline from exogenous lysoPC.
source: Perhaps to overcome this limitation, the parasite has evolved to scavenge most of the required choline from exogenous lysoPC (Brancucci et al., 2017; Wein et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Brancucci et al., 2017 and Wein et al., 2018.

claim: Active lysoPC metabolism into PC via the CDP-choline pathway prevents sexual commitment.
source: Intriguingly, lysoPC also acts as an environmental sensor that controls sexual differentiation in P. falciparum. Active lysoPC metabolism into PC via the CDP-choline pathway prevents sexual commitment, while in contrast limited availability of lysoPC reduces formation of asexual progeny and triggers differentiation into the transmissible gametocyte stages (Brancucci et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Brancucci et al., 2017.

claim: Limited availability of lysoPC reduces formation of asexual progeny and triggers differentiation into the transmissible gametocyte stages.
source: Intriguingly, lysoPC also acts as an environmental sensor that controls sexual differentiation in P. falciparum. Active lysoPC metabolism into PC via the CDP-choline pathway prevents sexual commitment, while in contrast limited availability of lysoPC reduces formation of asexual progeny and triggers differentiation into the transmissible gametocyte stages (Brancucci et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Brancucci et al., 2017.

claim: ∼68% of free choline in the parasite comes from exogenous lysoPC.
source: Metabolic labelling experiments showed that ∼68% of free choline in the parasite comes from exogenous lysoPC, indicating that the majority of the lysoPC is broken down to choline before entering PC synthesis (Brancucci et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Brancucci et al., 2017.

claim: The majority of lysoPC is broken down to choline before entering PC synthesis.
source: Metabolic labelling experiments showed that ∼68% of free choline in the parasite comes from exogenous lysoPC, indicating that the majority of the lysoPC is broken down to choline before entering PC synthesis (Brancucci et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference based on the metabolic labeling data cited from Brancucci et al., 2017.

claim: LysoPC breakdown to free choline requires a two-step hydrolysis reaction: deacylation of lysoPC by a putative lysophospholipase to give glycerophosphocholine (GPC) that is then hydrolysed by a glycerophosphodiester phosphodiesterase (GDPD) to generate choline and glycerol-3-phosphate (G3P).
source: LysoPC breakdown to free choline requires a two-step hydrolysis reaction: deacylation of lysoPC by a putative lysophospholipase to give glycerophosphocholine (GPC) that is then hydrolysed by a glycerophosphodiester phosphodiesterase (GDPD) to generate choline and glycerol-3-phosphate (G3P) (Figure 1).
evidence: This is based on knowledge of biochemical pathways and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: GPC catabolism by GDPD has been shown to maintain a choline supply for CDP-choline-dependent PC biosynthesis in model eukaryotes.
source: GPC catabolism by GDPD has been shown to maintain a choline supply for CDP-choline-dependent PC biosynthesis in model eukaryotes (Fernández-Murray and McMaster, 2005; Morita et al., 2016; Stewart et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fernández-Murray and McMaster, 2005; Morita et al., 2016; Stewart et al., 2012.

claim: Only one putative glycerophosphodiesterase gene (PfGDPD; PF3D7_1406300) has been identified in the malarial genome.
source: Only one putative glycerophosphodiesterase gene (PfGDPD; PF3D7_1406300) has been identified in the malarial genome (Denloye et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Denloye et al., 2012.

claim: The 475-residue predicted PfGDPD protein product has an N-terminal secretory signal peptide and a glycerophosphodiester phosphodiesterase domain (amino acid residues 24–466; InterPro entry IPR030395).
source: The 475-residue predicted protein product has an N-terminal secretory signal peptide and a glycerophosphodiester phosphodiesterase domain (amino acid residues 24–466; InterPro entry IPR030395), which likely adopts a triosephosphate isomerase (TIM) barrel alpha/beta fold (https://alphafold.ebi.ac.uk/entry/Q8IM31) (Jumper et al., 2021; Rao et al., 2006; Varadi et al., 2022).
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis and citations.

claim: The PfGDPD protein likely adopts a triosephosphate isomerase (TIM) barrel alpha/beta fold.
source: The 475-residue predicted protein product has an N-terminal secretory signal peptide and a glycerophosphodiester phosphodiesterase domain (amino acid residues 24–466; InterPro entry IPR030395), which likely adopts a triosephosphate isomerase (TIM) barrel alpha/beta fold (https://alphafold.ebi.ac.uk/entry/Q8IM31) (Jumper et al., 2021; Rao et al., 2006; Varadi et al., 2022).
evidence: This is based on AlphaFold predictions and citations to Jumper et al., 2021; Rao et al., 2006; Varadi et al., 2022.

claim: The PfGDPD protein shares homology with prokaryotic GDPDs and contains a characteristic small GDPD-specific insertion (residues 75–275) within the TIM barrel structure.
source: The protein shares homology with prokaryotic GDPDs and contains a characteristic small GDPD-specific insertion (residues 75–275) within the TIM barrel structure.
evidence: This is based on sequence and structural analysis.

claim: Recombinant PfGDPD has been shown to have hydrolytic activity towards GPC.
source: Recombinant PfGDPD has been shown to have hydrolytic activity towards GPC and localization studies have suggested that the protein is present in the parasite digestive vacuole (in which breakdown of host haemoglobin takes place), as well as the cytoplasm and parasitophorous vacuole (PV) (Denloye et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Denloye et al., 2012.

claim: Localization studies have suggested that PfGDPD is present in the parasite digestive vacuole, as well as the cytoplasm and parasitophorous vacuole (PV).
source: Recombinant PfGDPD has been shown to have hydrolytic activity towards GPC and localization studies have suggested that the protein is present in the parasite digestive vacuole (in which breakdown of host haemoglobin takes place), as well as the cytoplasm and parasitophorous vacuole (PV) (Denloye et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Denloye et al., 2012.

claim: Repeated failed attempts to disrupt the PfGDPD gene suggest its essentiality for asexual stage growth.
source: Repeated failed attempts to disrupt the PfGDPD gene (Denloye et al., 2012) and a genome-wide mutagenesis screen (Zhang et al., 2018) suggests its essentiality for asexual stage growth.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Denloye et al., 2012 and Zhang et al., 2018.

claim: A genome-wide mutagenesis screen suggests PfGDPD's essentiality for asexual stage growth.
source: Repeated failed attempts to disrupt the PfGDPD gene (Denloye et al., 2012) and a genome-wide mutagenesis screen (Zhang et al., 2018) suggests its essentiality for asexual stage growth.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2018.

claim: Endogenous PfGDPD tagged with GFP shows dual localization in the cytosol and PV.
source: Endogenous PfGDPD tagged with GFP shows dual localization in the cytosol and PV.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A with microscopy images.

claim: RAP-induced DiCre-mediated excision results in removal of the PfGDPD catalytic domain.
source: RAP-induced DiCre-mediated excision results in removal of the catalytic domain.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B as part of the experimental strategy.

claim: Diagnostic PCR 12 hr following mock- or RAP-treatment of ring-stage GDPD:HA:loxPint parasites confirms efficient gene excision.
source: Diagnostic PCR 12 hr following mock- or RAP-treatment of ring-stage GDPD:HA:loxPint parasites (representative of three independent experiments) confirms efficient gene excision.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C with PCR data.

claim: Western blots show successful RAP-induced ablation of PfGDPD expression in cycle 0 GDPD:HA:loxPint parasites.
source: Western blots (representative of two independent experiments) showing successful RAP-induced ablation of PfGDPD expression in cycle 0 GDPD:HA:loxPint parasites sampled at 24 hr and 48 hr post invasion and cycle 1 trophozoites (72 hr).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D with western blot data.

claim: IFA shows that expression of PfGDPD-HA is lost following RAP treatment in mature GDPD:HA:loxPint cycle 0 schizonts.
source: IFA of RAP-treated (+) and mock-treated (-) mature GDPD:HA:loxPint cycle 0 schizonts following mock- (-) or RAP-treatment (+) at ring-stage, showing that expression of PfGDPD-HA is lost following RAP treatment.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2E with immunofluorescence data.

claim: RAP-treatment results in loss of replication in two clonal lines, B4 and B8, of GDPD:HA:loxPint parasites.
source: RAP-treatment results in loss of replication in two clonal lines, B4 (black) and B8 (grey), of GDPD:HA:loxPint parasites (error bars, ± SD). Data shown are averages from triplicate biological replicates using different blood sources.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2F with growth curve data.

claim: Genetic complementation with an episomal, constitutively expressed mCherry-tagged PfGDPD fully restores growth of Rapa-treated GDPD:loxPint:HA:Neo-R parasites.
source: Genetic complementation with an episomal, constitutively expressed mCherry-tagged PfGDPD fully restores growth of Rapa-treated GDPD:loxPint:HA:Neo-R parasites.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2G with growth data.

claim: Mutant PfGDPD alleles carrying Ala substitutions of the catalytic H29 and H78 residues or the metal-binding residue E283 do not complement the growth defect.
source: In contrast, mutant PfGDPD alleles carrying Ala substitutions of the catalytic H29 and H78 residues or the metal-binding residue E283 do not complement.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2G with growth data.

claim: PfGDPD possesses two conserved predicted active site histidine residues (His29 and His78).
source: Like related GDPD enzymes, PfGDPD possesses two conserved predicted active site histidine residues (His29 and His78) and three metal-binding residues (Glu63, Asp65, and Glu283) that coordinate a Mg2+ cation in the active site and are likely required for activity (Shi et al., 2008).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and citation to Shi et al., 2008.

claim: PfGDPD possesses three metal-binding residues (Glu63, Asp65, and Glu283) that coordinate a Mg2+ cation in the active site.
source: Like related GDPD enzymes, PfGDPD possesses two conserved predicted active site histidine residues (His29 and His78) and three metal-binding residues (Glu63, Asp65, and Glu283) that coordinate a Mg2+ cation in the active site and are likely required for activity (Shi et al., 2008).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and citation to Shi et al., 2008.

claim: Recombinant PfGDPD has been previously shown to display Mg2+-dependent glycerophosphodiesterase activity.
source: Consistent with this, recombinant PfGDPD has been previously shown to display Mg2+-dependent glycerophosphodiesterase activity (Denloye et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Denloye et al., 2012.

claim: Mutagenesis of key residues H29, H78, and E283 completely abolished rescue of parasite growth upon disruption of the chromosomal gene.
source: Mutagenesis of these key residues did not alter the expression or subcellular localization of the transgenic PfGDPD:H29A:H78A:E283A protein (Figure 2—figure supplement 3F and G) but completely abolished rescue of parasite growth upon disruption of the chromosomal gene (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 3F and G.

claim: The essential function of PfGDPD depends on its catalytic activity.
source: These results strongly suggest that the essential function of PfGDPD depends on its catalytic activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mutagenesis and complementation data.

claim: PfGDPD-null mutant parasites developed normally throughout the erythrocytic cycle of treatment (cycle 0) and were able to egress and invade fresh RBCs.
source: Mutant parasites developed normally throughout the erythrocytic cycle of treatment (cycle 0) and were able to egress and invade fresh RBCs.
evidence: This is based on microscopy and flow cytometry observations described in the text.

claim: Parasitaemia in the PfGDPD-null cultures was lower than controls in cycle 1 (25% vs 34%).
source: However, looking more closely at the transition between cycle 0 and cycle 1, we observed that parasitaemia in the PfGDPD-null cultures was lower than controls in cycle 1 (25% vs 34%) (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B with quantitative data.

claim: Short-term replication assays confirmed lower fold increases in parasitaemia in the RAP-treated parasites in the transition from cycle 0 to cycle 1.
source: Short-term replication assays under both shaking and static conditions confirmed lower fold increases in parasitaemia in the RAP-treated parasites in the transition from cycle 0 to cycle 1 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C with replication assay data.

claim: Mean numbers of merozoites in mature cycle 0 GDPD-null schizonts were slightly lower than wild-type schizonts.
source: Mean numbers of merozoites in mature cycle 0 GDPD-null schizonts were slightly lower than wild-type schizonts, perhaps contributing to the lower replication rate (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3D with merozoite count data.

claim: By ∼24 hr into cycle 1 most of the PfGDPD-null trophozoites were developmentally arrested, at which point a decrease in DNA content was detected.
source: By ∼24 hr into cycle 1 most of the PfGDPD-null trophozoites were developmentally arrested, at which point we also detected a decrease in DNA content (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A with flow cytometry data.

claim: The majority (∼88%) of PfGDPD-null mutants failed to reach schizont stage in cycle 1, instead arresting as rings or trophozoites.
source: Microscopic quantification of the various developmental stages at a range of selected time points confirmed that the majority (∼88%) of PfGDPD-null mutants failed to reach schizont stage in cycle 1, instead arresting as rings or trophozoites (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B with stage quantification data.

claim: TEM analysis of the growth-stalled cycle 1 trophozoites did not reveal any discernible abnormalities in morphology or membrane formation.
source: Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) analysis of the growth-stalled cycle 1 trophozoites did not reveal any discernible abnormalities in morphology or membrane formation.
evidence: This is based on TEM observations described in the text.

claim: Noticeably decreased haemozoin crystal formation was observed in the digestive vacuole of PfGDPD-null parasites in all developmental stages.
source: However, we observed noticeably decreased haemozoin crystal formation in the digestive vacuole of PfGDPD-null parasites in all developmental stages (Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1 with TEM images.

claim: Haemozoin content of PfGDPD-null parasites was significantly lower than in wildtype parasites both in 44 hpi schizonts in cycle 0 and in 24 hpi trophozoites in cycle 1.
source: Haemozoin content of PfGDPD-null parasites was also significantly lower than in wildtype parasites both in 44 hpi schizonts in cycle 0 (despite normal growth progression) and in 24 hpi trophozoites in cycle 1 when quantified using polarization microscopy (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3F with polarization microscopy quantification.

claim: Upon RAP-treatment at ring stage to ablate PfGDPD expression, parasites were able to develop normally to schizonts in cycle 0, perhaps due to the presence of residual enzyme.
source: Collectively, these data showed that upon RAP-treatment at ring stage to ablate PfGDPD expression, parasites were able to develop normally to schizonts in cycle 0, perhaps due to the presence of residual enzyme, but showed defective growth and reduced replication rate at the schizont stages and a definitive developmental arrest at trophozoite stages in the following cycle.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the data presented in Figure 3.

claim: PfGDPD-null parasites showed defective growth and reduced replication rate at the schizont stages and a definitive developmental arrest at trophozoite stages in cycle 1.
source: Collectively, these data showed that upon RAP-treatment at ring stage to ablate PfGDPD expression, parasites were able to develop normally to schizonts in cycle 0, perhaps due to the presence of residual enzyme, but showed defective growth and reduced replication rate at the schizont stages and a definitive developmental arrest at trophozoite stages in the following cycle.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the data presented in Figure 3.

claim: In the presence of supraphysiological concentrations of choline, the RAP-treated GDPD:loxPint:HA parasites retained normal morphology.
source: This was indeed the case; in the presence of supraphysiological concentrations of choline (but not glycerophosphocholine, ethanolamine or serine), the RAP-treated GDPD:loxPint:HA parasites retained normal morphology (Figure 4A) and were able to proliferate, albeit at a ∼30% slower rate than controls (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A with microscopy images.

claim: In the presence of supraphysiological concentrations of choline, the RAP-treated GDPD:loxPint:HA parasites were able to proliferate, albeit at a ∼30% slower rate than controls.
source: This was indeed the case; in the presence of supraphysiological concentrations of choline (but not glycerophosphocholine, ethanolamine or serine), the RAP-treated GDPD:loxPint:HA parasites retained normal morphology (Figure 4A) and were able to proliferate, albeit at a ∼30% slower rate than controls (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B and C with growth data.

claim: Glycerophosphocholine, ethanolamine or serine did not rescue the developmental defect of PfGDPD-null parasites.
source: This was indeed the case; in the presence of supraphysiological concentrations of choline (but not glycerophosphocholine, ethanolamine or serine), the RAP-treated GDPD:loxPint:HA parasites retained normal morphology (Figure 4A) and were able to proliferate, albeit at a ∼30% slower rate than controls (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C with growth data.

claim: The emergent parasite population in the choline-rescued RAP-treated cultures were indeed PfGDPD-null parasites (and not residual non-excised parasites).
source: Confirmation that the emergent parasite population in the choline-rescued RAP-treated cultures were indeed PfGDPD-null parasites (and not residual non-excised parasites) was obtained using IFA and whole genome sequencing (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4D with IFA and sequencing data.

claim: Continuous supplementation of the growth medium with choline allowed maintenance of the PfGDPD-null parasites indefinitely.
source: Continuous supplementation of the growth medium with choline allowed us to maintain the PfGDPD-null parasites indefinitely, and even to isolate clonal lines through limiting dilution.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations described in the text.

claim: Growth of PfGDPD-null clones remained completely dependent on exogenous choline.
source: Growth of these clones remained completely dependent on exogenous choline (Figure 4E), with removal of choline resulting in the appearance of developmental defects and growth arrest within ∼24 hr.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4E with growth data.

claim: Removal of choline from PfGDPD-null parasites resulted in the appearance of developmental defects and growth arrest within ∼24 hr.
source: Growth of these clones remained completely dependent on exogenous choline (Figure 4E), with removal of choline resulting in the appearance of developmental defects and growth arrest within ∼24 hr.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4E with microscopy and growth data.

claim: Choline concentrations of 500 µM or higher were required to sustain parasite growth at near wild-type levels.
source: Further characterization of the choline dependency using PfGDPD-null clone G1 showed that choline concentrations of 500 µM or higher were required to sustain parasite growth at near wild-type levels (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4F with dose-response data.

claim: Exogenous choline can substitute for a functional PfGDPD gene, directly implicating PfGDPD in choline scavenging.
source: Collectively, these data clearly showed that exogenous choline can substitute for a functional PfGDPD gene, directly implicating PfGDPD in choline scavenging.
evidence: This is an inference based on the choline rescue experiments.

claim: Quantitative lipidome analysis detected a total of 134 PL species in both RAP- and DMSO-treated mature GDPD:HA:loxPint schizonts.
source: Quantitative lipidome analysis detected a total of 134 PL species in both RAP- and DMSO-treated mature GDPD:HA:loxPint schizonts.
evidence: This is based on lipidomic analysis described in the text.

claim: Decreases in abundance in the RAP-treated parasites were observed for all the major PL classes, including PC, PS, phosphatidylethanolamine (PE) and phosphatidylinositol (PI).
source: Of these, we observed decreases in abundance in the RAP-treated parasites of all the major PL classes, including PC, PS, phosphatidylethanolamine (PE) and phosphatidylinositol (PI) (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A with lipidomic data.

claim: The reduction in several PC species (10 out of 22 detected species) was significant (p<0.05) but less than 1.5-fold.
source: The reduction in several PC species (10 out of 22 detected species) was significant (p<0.05) but less than 1.5-fold, while levels of most PE, PS, and PI species were more drastically reduced.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of lipidomic data.

claim: Greater than two-fold reductions were evident in seven lipid species: PE(32:3), PE(36:5), PE(32:32), PS(34:1), PS(18:1/18:2), PS(18:1/18:1), PS(18:0/18:1), and PS(34:1).
source: Greater than two-fold reductions were evident in the case of seven species (PE(32:3), PE(36:5), PE(32:32), PS(34:1), PS(18:1/18:2), PS(18:1/18:1), PS(18:0/18:1), and PS(34:1)).
evidence: This is based on lipidomic analysis data.

claim: These changes in lipid levels were accompanied by substantial enrichment of DAG levels in the RAP-treated parasites, with 15 out of 27 species showing significantly higher levels compared to controls.
source: These changes were accompanied by substantial enrichment of DAG levels in the RAP-treated parasites, with 15 out of 27 species showing significantly higher levels compared to controls.
evidence: This is based on lipidomic analysis data.

claim: Under choline-limiting conditions the parasite can switch from the CDP-choline pathway to the SDPM pathway to produce PC.
source: Previous work has shown that under choline-limiting conditions the parasite can switch from the CDP-choline pathway to the SDPM pathway to produce PC (Wein et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wein et al., 2018.

claim: Depleted lysoPC levels cause upregulation of PfPMT.
source: Similarly, depleted lysoPC levels cause upregulation of PfPMT (Brancucci et al., 2018; Brancucci et al., 2017; Wein et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Brancucci et al., 2018; Brancucci et al., 2017; Wein et al., 2018.

claim: A similar switch from CDP-choline to SDPM pathway occurs in PfGDPD-null parasites in order to maintain PC biosynthesis.
source: We interpreted our lipidomics results as suggesting that a similar switch occurs in PfGDPD-null parasites in order to maintain PC biosynthesis, at the expense of most of the available serine and ethanolamine pool being redirected towards PC biosynthesis, in turn resulting in lowered PE and PS production.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lipidomic data.

claim: In PfGDPD-null parasites, most of the available serine and ethanolamine pool is redirected towards PC biosynthesis, resulting in lowered PE and PS production.
source: We interpreted our lipidomics results as suggesting that a similar switch occurs in PfGDPD-null parasites in order to maintain PC biosynthesis, at the expense of most of the available serine and ethanolamine pool being redirected towards PC biosynthesis, in turn resulting in lowered PE and PS production.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lipidomic data.

claim: The disturbance in precursor availability likely reduces usage of DAG, resulting in its accumulation.
source: This disturbance in precursor availability likely reduces usage of DAG, the primary backbone for glycerolipid and neutral lipid production, resulting in its accumulation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lipidomic data showing DAG accumulation.

claim: 20-40% of the detectable PC species were labelled with isotope in both RAP- and mock-treated GDPD:HA:loxPint parasites in cycle 0.
source: As shown in Figure 5B, 20-40% of the detectable PC species were labelled with the isotope in both treatment groups.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B with metabolic labeling data.

claim: Only a small, statistically insignificant decrease was observed in the labelled proportions for 5 out of 9 PC species detected in the RAP-treated parasites compared to the controls in cycle 0.
source: Only a small, statistically insignificant decrease was observed in the labelled proportions for 5 out of 9 PC species detected in the RAP-treated parasites compared to the controls, indicating no effects of RAP-treatment on lysoPC metabolism.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of metabolic labeling data.

claim: A consistent and significant decrease (25–50%) in labelling of 10 out of 13 PC species was observed in the choline-starved PfGDPD-null G1 parasites compared to the B4 controls.
source: However, a consistent and significant decrease (25–50%) in labelling of 10 out of 13 PC species was observed in the choline-starved PfGDPD-null G1 parasites compared to the B4 controls.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C with metabolic labeling data.

claim: PfGDPD plays an important role in metabolism of exogenous lysoPC for PC synthesis.
source: These results strongly suggest that PfGDPD plays an important role in metabolism of exogenous lysoPC for PC synthesis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the metabolic labeling experiments.

claim: Several PC species (7 out of 14 PC species) were significantly depleted in choline-starved G1 parasites.
source: This revealed large-scale changes in phospholipid and neutral lipid species in the choline-starved G1 parasites. Several PC species (7 out of 14 PC species) were significantly depleted in choline-starved G1 parasites, with three species - PC(16:0/18:3), PC(16:0/16:1) and PC(16:0/20:5) - decreased in abundance more than two-fold.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C with lipidomic data.

claim: Three PC species - PC(16:0/18:3), PC(16:0/16:1) and PC(16:0/20:5) - decreased in abundance more than two-fold in choline-starved G1 parasites.
source: This revealed large-scale changes in phospholipid and neutral lipid species in the choline-starved G1 parasites. Several PC species (7 out of 14 PC species) were significantly depleted in choline-starved G1 parasites, with three species - PC(16:0/18:3), PC(16:0/16:1) and PC(16:0/20:5) - decreased in abundance more than two-fold.
evidence: This is based on lipidomic analysis data.

claim: The depletion of PC species in choline-starved G1 parasites was accompanied by a concomitant increase in levels of lysoPC (LPC) species, LPC(16:0) and LPC(18:0).
source: This was accompanied by a concomitant increase in levels of lysoPC (LPC) species, LPC(16:0) and LPC(18:0).
evidence: This is based on lipidomic analysis data.

claim: Significant accumulation of DAG species (DAG(18:0/20:4) and DAG(18:0/22:5)) was observed in choline-starved G1 parasites, pointing to Kennedy pathway dysfunction.
source: Similar to what we observed in PfGDPD-null schizonts, we noticed significant accumulation of DAG species (DAG(18:0/20:4) and DAG(18:0/22:5)), pointing to Kennedy pathway dysfunction.
evidence: This is based on lipidomic analysis data and inference about pathway dysfunction.

claim: Several phosphatidylglycerol (PG(18:1/18:2), PG(18:1/18:1) and PG(36:3)) and acyl-phosphatidylglycerol (acyl-PG) species were notably depleted in choline-starved G1 parasites.
source: Several phosphatidylglycerol (PG(18:1/18:2), PG(18:1/18:1) and PG(36:3)) and acyl-phosphatidylglycerol (acyl-PG) species were also notably depleted.
evidence: This is based on lipidomic analysis data.

claim: All PI species detected were significantly depleted in choline-starved G1 parasites.
source: All PI species detected were significantly depleted in choline-starved G1 parasites, as observed in PfGDPD-null schizonts.
evidence: This is based on lipidomic analysis data.

claim: In contrast to the PfGDPD-null schizonts, most PE and PS species were unchanged between the mutant G1 parasites and the B4 controls.
source: On the other hand, in contrast to the PfGDPD-null schizonts, most PE and PS species were unchanged between the mutant G1 parasites and the B4 controls.
evidence: This is based on lipidomic analysis data.

claim: Several species of TAG were significantly depleted in choline-starved G1 parasites, with 8 species showing almost two to fivefold decrease in abundance.
source: Another notable feature was the significant depletion of several species of TAG in choline-starved G1 parasites, with 8 species showing almost two to fivefold decrease in abundance.
evidence: This is based on lipidomic analysis data.

claim: A twofold increase in the abundance of the betaine lipid diacylglyceryl-N,N,N-trimethylhomoserine (DGTS) was observed in G1 parasites.
source: We also observed a twofold increase in the abundance of the betaine lipid diacylglyceryl-N,N,N-trimethylhomoserine (DGTS) in G1 parasites (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B with lipidomic data.

claim: DGTS functions as a substitute for PC in certain algal species including Chlamydomonas reinhardtii.
source: This unusual lipid, which functions as a substitute for PC in certain algal species including Chlamydomonas reinhardtii (Giroud et al., 1988; Sato et al., 1995), has not been previously detected in malaria parasites.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Giroud et al., 1988 and Sato et al., 1995.

claim: DGTS has not been previously detected in malaria parasites.
source: This unusual lipid, which functions as a substitute for PC in certain algal species including Chlamydomonas reinhardtii (Giroud et al., 1988; Sato et al., 1995), has not been previously detected in malaria parasites.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the finding.

claim: The MS/MS spectra of three DGTS species (DGTS(34:1), DGTS(35:1) and DGTS(38:2)) in the samples matched that of a commercially available DGTS standard (DGTS(32:0)).
source: We were able to match the MS/MS spectra of three DGTS species (DGTS(34:1), DGTS(35:1) and DGTS(38:2)) in our samples to that of a commercially available DGTS standard (DGTS(32:0)) thus confirming correct identification of the species (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2 with MS/MS spectra.

claim: Incubating immobilised PfGDPD-HA pulled-down from control GDPD:HA:loxPint parasites with GPC resulted in the time-dependent appearance of choline with a concomitant decrease in GPC levels.
source: Incubating immobilised PfGDPD-HA pulled-down from control GDPD:HA:loxPint parasites with GPC resulted in the time-dependent appearance of choline with a concomitant decrease in GPC levels (Figure 6).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6 with enzymatic assay data.

claim: The rate of choline appearance was greatly decreased using pull-downs from PfGDPD-null parasites (RAP-treated GDPD:HA:loxPint parasites or the G1 clone).
source: As expected, the rate of choline appearance was greatly decreased using pull-downs from PfGDPD-null parasites (RAP-treated GDPD:HA:loxPint parasites or the G1 clone).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6 with enzymatic assay data.

claim: PfGDPD can release choline from GPC.
source: These results provide direct evidence that PfGDPD can release choline from GPC.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the enzymatic assay data.

claim: PfGDPD is essential for parasite growth in NF54 parasites.
source: This showed that PfGDPD is essential for parasite growth in NF54 parasites (Figure 7A), with gene disruption producing a similar developmental defect at trophozoite stage as that observed in the GDPD:HA:loxPint line (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7A with growth data.

claim: Gene disruption of PfGDPD in NF54 parasites produced a similar developmental defect at trophozoite stage as that observed in the GDPD:HA:loxPint line.
source: This showed that PfGDPD is essential for parasite growth in NF54 parasites (Figure 7A), with gene disruption producing a similar developmental defect at trophozoite stage as that observed in the GDPD:HA:loxPint line (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7B with microscopy images.

claim: There was no detectable induction of gametocyte formation following PfGDPD disruption in NF54 parasites.
source: There was no detectable induction of gametocyte formation.
evidence: This is based on microscopy observations described in the text.

claim: The loss of PfGDPD causes a severe block in PC synthesis resulting in the death of asexual parasites before they get to form gametocytes.
source: This result implies that the loss of PfGDPD causes a severe block in PC synthesis resulting in the death of asexual parasites before they get to form gametocytes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of gametocyte formation.

claim: Host serum lysoPC is well established as the main precursor for PC synthesis in the parasite.
source: Host serum lysoPC, well established as the main precursor for PC synthesis in the parasite (Brancucci et al., 2017; Wein et al., 2018), can enter the parasitized erythrocyte efficiently through rapid exchange (Dushianthan et al., 2019) after which it may be transported into the parasite by exported phospholipid transfer proteins (van Ooij et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Brancucci et al., 2017 and Wein et al., 2018.

claim: LysoPC can enter the parasitized erythrocyte efficiently through rapid exchange.
source: Host serum lysoPC, well established as the main precursor for PC synthesis in the parasite (Brancucci et al., 2017; Wein et al., 2018), can enter the parasitized erythrocyte efficiently through rapid exchange (Dushianthan et al., 2019) after which it may be transported into the parasite by exported phospholipid transfer proteins (van Ooij et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Dushianthan et al., 2019.

claim: LysoPC may be transported into the parasite by exported phospholipid transfer proteins.
source: Host serum lysoPC, well established as the main precursor for PC synthesis in the parasite (Brancucci et al., 2017; Wein et al., 2018), can enter the parasitized erythrocyte efficiently through rapid exchange (Dushianthan et al., 2019) after which it may be transported into the parasite by exported phospholipid transfer proteins (van Ooij et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to van Ooij et al., 2013.

claim: Ablation of PfGDPD expression produced a phenotypic defect during trophozoite development as either a direct or general stress response to disrupted PC synthesis.
source: Ablation of PfGDPD expression produced a phenotypic defect during trophozoite development as either a direct or general stress response to disrupted PC synthesis, similar to that observed upon inhibition of other enzymes involved in CDP-choline pathway (González-Bulnes et al., 2011; Serrán-Aguilera et al., 2016; Contet et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed phenotype and citations to similar findings.

claim: Previous transcriptional studies have shown that PfGDPD is expressed early in the erythrocytic cycle.
source: Unsurprisingly for an enzyme playing a key role in membrane biogenesis, previous transcriptional studies have shown that PfGDPD is expressed early in the erythrocytic cycle.
evidence: This is based on prior transcriptional studies.

claim: DiCre-mediated disruption of PfGDPD results in parasites that undergo normal development in the erythrocytic cycle of RAP-treatment (cycle 0) likely due to the presence of residual enzyme produced early during ring stage development.
source: Our observation that DiCre-mediated disruption of PfGDPD results in parasites that undergo normal development in the erythrocytic cycle of RAP-treatment (cycle 0) is therefore likely due to the presence of residual enzyme produced early during ring stage development (prior to gene excision) and persisting throughout that cycle.
evidence: This is an inference based on the timing of gene excision and protein expression.

claim: PfGDPD-null parasites that were rendered completely devoid of the enzyme through propagation for several cycles in choline-supplemented media exhibited maturation defects within ∼24 hr of choline removal.
source: In support of this, PfGDPD-null parasites that were rendered completely devoid of the enzyme through propagation for several cycles in choline-supplemented media exhibited maturation defects within ∼24 hr of choline removal.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations described in the text.

claim: PfGDPD acts as a glycerophosphocholine phosphodiesterase and releases choline from the intermediary GPC during lysoPC breakdown.
source: We infer that PfGDPD acts as a glycerophosphocholine phosphodiesterase and releases choline from the intermediary GPC during lysoPC breakdown from the following findings.
evidence: This is an inference based on multiple lines of evidence presented in the manuscript.

claim: Site-directed mutagenesis showed that PfGDPD retains the same essential catalytic sites and metal-ion dependency as a bacterial choline-releasing GDPD enzyme.
source: First, site-directed mutagenesis showed that PfGDPD retains the same essential catalytic sites and metal-ion dependency as a bacterial choline-releasing GDPD enzyme (Shi et al., 2008).
evidence: This is based on mutagenesis experiments and citation to Shi et al., 2008.

claim: Supplying an excess of choline can rescue the growth of parasites in lysoPC-deprived conditions.
source: Previous work has shown that supplying an excess of choline can rescue the growth of parasites in lysoPC-deprived conditions (Witola et al., 2008; Wein et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Witola et al., 2008 and Wein et al., 2018.

claim: High concentrations of exogenous choline partially surpass the bottleneck in choline transport across the red blood cell membrane.
source: High concentrations of exogenous choline partially surpass the bottleneck in choline transport across the red blood cell membrane (Biagini et al., 2004) and increase choline influx through infected RBCs (Kirk et al., 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Biagini et al., 2004 and Kirk et al., 1991.

claim: LysoPC-deprived parasites can readily take up exogenous choline and use it for PC synthesis.
source: LysoPC-deprived parasites can readily take up this choline and use it for PC synthesis as shown by previous metabolic labelling studies (Brancucci et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Brancucci et al., 2017.

claim: The complete dependence of PfGDPD-null mutants on exogenous choline despite the abundant presence of lysoPC in the culture media is a further confirmation that ablating PfGDPD function interferes with choline acquisition from lysoPC.
source: This complete dependence on exogenous choline despite the abundant presence of lysoPC (amounting to ∼17% of total lipid content Garcia-Gonzalo and Izpisúa Belmonte, 2008) in the Albumax II-supplemented culture media used in our studies or supplementation with GPC, is a further confirmation that ablating PfGDPD function interferes with choline acquisition from lysoPC and mimics a lysoPC-deprived state.
evidence: This is an inference based on the choline rescue experiments.

claim: Ablating PfGDPD function mimics a lysoPC-deprived state.
source: This complete dependence on exogenous choline despite the abundant presence of lysoPC (amounting to ∼17% of total lipid content Garcia-Gonzalo and Izpisúa Belmonte, 2008) in the Albumax II-supplemented culture media used in our studies or supplementation with GPC, is a further confirmation that ablating PfGDPD function interferes with choline acquisition from lysoPC and mimics a lysoPC-deprived state.
evidence: This is an inference based on the choline rescue experiments.

claim: Loss of PfGDPD reduced – but did not eliminate – incorporation of lysoPC-derived choline.
source: Loss of PfGDPD also reduced – but did not eliminate – incorporation of lysoPC-derived choline.
evidence: This is based on metabolic labeling experiments.

claim: Alternate pathways such as direct lysoPC acylation into PC via the Lands' cycle, two acylation steps to convert GPC to PC or the SDPM pathway may contribute to PC synthesis under choline-starved conditions.
source: This suggests that alternate pathways such as direct lysoPC acylation into PC via the Lands' cycle, two acylation steps to convert GPC to PC or the SDPM pathway may contribute to PC synthesis under choline-starved conditions.
evidence: This is speculation based on the incomplete block of lysoPC incorporation.

claim: PfGDPD-mediated choline release from lysoPC remains the primary, indispensable pathway to meet the choline requirements of the intraerythrocytic parasite.
source: However, our results strongly suggest that PfGDPD-mediated choline release from lysoPC remains the primary, indispensable pathway to meet the choline requirements of the intraerythrocytic parasite.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: The observed depletion of TAG in choline-starved PfGDPD-null parasites was unexpected since there is no previously reported role for a glycerophosphodiesterase in neutral lipid metabolism.
source: The observed depletion of TAG in choline-starved PfGDPD-null parasites was unexpected since there is no previously reported role for a glycerophosphodiesterase in neutral lipid metabolism.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the finding.

claim: An intense phase of de novo TAG biosynthesis from DAG is known to accompany trophozoite development.
source: An intense phase of de novo TAG biosynthesis from DAG is known to accompany trophozoite development (Palacpac et al., 2004; Vielemeyer et al., 2004), followed by a rapid hydrolysis of TAG in mature schizonts resulting in localized release of fatty acids essential for merozoite maturation prior to egress (Gulati et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Palacpac et al., 2004 and Vielemeyer et al., 2004.

claim: Rapid hydrolysis of TAG in mature schizonts results in localized release of fatty acids essential for merozoite maturation prior to egress.
source: An intense phase of de novo TAG biosynthesis from DAG is known to accompany trophozoite development (Palacpac et al., 2004; Vielemeyer et al., 2004), followed by a rapid hydrolysis of TAG in mature schizonts resulting in localized release of fatty acids essential for merozoite maturation prior to egress (Gulati et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gulati et al., 2015.

claim: A block in PC synthesis can either cause the depletion of the PC-derived DAG pool and block TAG synthesis, or lead to increased metabolism of TAG to feed fatty acids into the compensatory Lands' cycle that acylates lysoPC to PC.
source: A block in PC synthesis can either cause the depletion of the PC-derived DAG pool and block TAG synthesis, or lead to increased metabolism of TAG to feed fatty acids into the compensatory Lands' cycle that acylates lysoPC to PC (Caviglia et al., 2004; Moessinger et al., 2014).
evidence: This is speculation based on knowledge from other organisms and citations to Caviglia et al., 2004 and Moessinger et al., 2014.

claim: Studies in other organisms increasingly show a bidirectional link between TAG and PC synthesis in which PC-derived DAG is used for TAG synthesis and TAG-derived fatty acids are used for synthesis of PC through the Lands' cycle.
source: Studies in other organisms increasingly show a bidirectional link between TAG and PC synthesis in which PC-derived DAG is used for TAG synthesis and TAG-derived fatty acids are used for synthesis of PC through the Lands' cycle (Bates and Browse, 2011; Caviglia et al., 2004; Moessinger et al., 2014; Soudant et al., 2000; van der Veen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bates and Browse, 2011; Caviglia et al., 2004; Moessinger et al., 2014; Soudant et al., 2000; van der Veen et al., 2012.

claim: The reduced haemozoin formation in GDPD-null parasites could be a result of the decrease in TAG levels.
source: The reduced haemozoin formation in GDPD-null parasites could also be a result of this decrease in TAG levels.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed phenotype.

claim: Neutral lipids have been suggested to play a role in the parasite haem detoxification pathway and promote haemozoin formation.
source: Neutral lipids have been suggested to play a role in the parasite haem detoxification pathway and promote haemozoin formation (Hoang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hoang et al., 2010.

claim: Knockdown of a P. falciparum lysophospholipase results in reduced TAG levels, reduced haemozoin formation and a block in trophozoite development.
source: Indeed it was recently shown that knockdown of a P. falciparum lysophospholipase results in reduced TAG levels, reduced haemozoin formation and a block in trophozoite development (Asad et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Asad et al., 2021.

claim: The betaine lipid DGTS is prevalently found in photosynthetic organisms like green algae, mosses and ferns.
source: Our lipidomics analysis identified the betaine lipid DGTS, prevalently found in photosynthetic organisms like green algae, mosses and ferns (Giroud et al., 1988; Sato et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Giroud et al., 1988 and Sato et al., 1995.

claim: DGTS has been detected in the lipidome of Chromera velia and Vitrella brassicaformis, the algal ancestors of apicomplexan parasites.
source: DGTS has also been detected in the lipidome of Chromera velia and Vitrella brassicaformis, the algal ancestors of apicomplexan parasites (Tomčala et al., 2017) but has not been previously reported in Plasmodium.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Tomčala et al., 2017.

claim: Accumulation of DGTS in choline-starved PfGDPD-null parasites is strikingly reminiscent of reports of DGTS synthesis as a non-phosphorous substitute for PC in fungi and marine bacteria under phosphate- or choline-starved conditions.
source: Accumulation of DGTS in choline-starved PfGDPD-null parasites is strikingly reminiscent of reports of DGTS synthesis as a non-phosphorous substitute for PC in fungi and marine bacteria under phosphate- or choline-starved conditions (Geiger et al., 2013; Riekhof et al., 2014; Sebastián et al., 2016; Senik et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Geiger et al., 2013; Riekhof et al., 2014; Sebastián et al., 2016; Senik et al., 2015.

claim: The methyl donor S-adenosyl methionine (SAM) is capable of providing both the homo-serine moiety and the methyl groups to produce DGTS from DAG.
source: The methyl donor S-adenosyl methionine (SAM) is capable of providing both the homo-serine moiety and the methyl groups to produce DGTS from DAG (Moore et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Moore et al., 2001.

claim: Enzymes involved in SAM synthesis are upregulated in lysoPC-limiting conditions.
source: Enzymes involved in SAM synthesis are upregulated in lysoPC-limiting conditions and diversion of SAM pools from histone methylation towards compensatory PC biosynthetic pathways is the primary link between PC metabolism and sexual differentiation in P. falciparum (Harris et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Harris et al., 2022.

claim: Diversion of SAM pools from histone methylation towards compensatory PC biosynthetic pathways is the primary link between PC metabolism and sexual differentiation in P. falciparum.
source: Enzymes involved in SAM synthesis are upregulated in lysoPC-limiting conditions and diversion of SAM pools from histone methylation towards compensatory PC biosynthetic pathways is the primary link between PC metabolism and sexual differentiation in P. falciparum (Harris et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Harris et al., 2022.

claim: Blocking PC biosynthesis in P. falciparum may trigger a compensatory pathway that produces DGTS as a functional substitute for PC in the parasite.
source: It is therefore tempting to speculate that blocking PC biosynthesis in P. falciparum triggers a compensatory pathway that produces DGTS as a functional substitute for PC in the parasite.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed DGTS accumulation.

claim: PfGDPD could potentially perform similar functions in both the PV and parasite cytosol by facilitating the breakdown of exogenous lysoPC.
source: PfGDPD could potentially perform similar functions in both compartments by facilitating the breakdown of exogenous lysoPC both within the PV and within the parasite cytosol (Brancucci et al., 2017).
evidence: This is speculation based on the localization data and citation to Brancucci et al., 2017.

claim: This scale of enzyme activity may be essential for the parasite to meet its choline needs, given the high levels of PC synthesis during parasite development.
source: This scale of enzyme activity may be essential for the parasite to meet its choline needs, given the high levels of PC synthesis during parasite development and its crucial importance for intraerythrocytic membrane biogenesis.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed essentiality of PfGDPD.

claim: PfGDPD may have other roles during asexual stages such as temporal and localised recycling of intracellular PC or GPC by the PfGDPD fraction expressed in the cytosol.
source: PfGDPD may also have other roles during asexual stages such as temporal and localised recycling of intracellular PC or GPC by the PfGDPD fraction expressed in the cytosol.
evidence: This is speculation about additional functions of PfGDPD.

claim: Ligand docking simulations do not rule out additional catalytic activity of PfGDPD towards other glycerophosphodiester substrates such as glycerophosphoethanolamine and glycerophosphoserine.
source: Finally, our ligand docking simulations do not rule out additional catalytic activity towards other glycerophosphodiester substrates such as glycerophosphoethanolamine and glycerophosphoserine (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A, B).
evidence: This is based on in silico docking simulations shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A, B.

claim: Orthologs of PfGDPD form a Haematozoan-specific ortholog group (OG6_139464) that encompasses only blood parasites that have an intra-erythrocytic stage.
source: Orthologs of PfGDPD form a Haematozoan-specific ortholog group (OG6_139464 in OrthoMCL DB release 6.4) that encompasses only blood parasites that have an intra-erythrocytic stage, that is the genera Babesia, Theileria, Plasmodium and Hepatocystis (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2C with phylogenetic analysis.

claim: This entire ortholog group could have a conserved role in choline acquisition for the critical process of PC biosynthesis to support an intra-erythrocytic lifestyle.
source: We speculate that this entire ortholog group could have a conserved role in choline acquisition for the critical process of PC biosynthesis to support an intra-erythrocytic lifestyle.
evidence: This is speculation based on the phylogenetic analysis.

claim: PC biosynthesis is the main biosynthetic process in blood stages of Babesia.
source: PC biosynthesis is the main biosynthetic process in blood stages of Babesia (Florin-Christensen et al., 2000) and compounds that inhibit PC biosynthesis have been shown to have anti-parasite activity against Babesia and Theileria blood stages (AbouLaila et al., 2014; Gopalakrishnan et al., 2016; Maji et al., 2019; Richier et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Florin-Christensen et al., 2000.

claim: Compounds that inhibit PC biosynthesis have been shown to have anti-parasite activity against Babesia and Theileria blood stages.
source: PC biosynthesis is the main biosynthetic process in blood stages of Babesia (Florin-Christensen et al., 2000) and compounds that inhibit PC biosynthesis have been shown to have anti-parasite activity against Babesia and Theileria blood stages (AbouLaila et al., 2014; Gopalakrishnan et al., 2016; Maji et al., 2019; Richier et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to AbouLaila et al., 2014; Gopalakrishnan et al., 2016; Maji et al., 2019; Richier et al., 2006.

claim: A malaria parasite choline-releasing glycerophosphodiesterase catalyses a critical step in choline acquisition from exogenous lysoPC.
source: In conclusion, we have demonstrated that a malaria parasite choline-releasing glycerophosphodiesterase catalyses a critical step in choline acquisition from exogenous lysoPC.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: PfGDPD-mediated procurement of choline is indispensable for normal PC biosynthesis and asexual blood stage development in the parasite.
source: Since PfGDPD-mediated procurement of choline is indispensable for normal PC biosynthesis and asexual blood stage development in the parasite, it may represent a potential new drug target.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing essentiality.

claim: PfGDPD may represent a potential new drug target.
source: Since PfGDPD-mediated procurement of choline is indispensable for normal PC biosynthesis and asexual blood stage development in the parasite, it may represent a potential new drug target.
evidence: This is speculation about the translational potential of the findings.
